reference.source: The Adult and Pediatric Spine (Rothman-Simeone) / Apley and Solomon's System of Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: The ligamentum flavum connects adjacent laminae and is normally rich in elastin, giving it its characteristic recoil; hypertrophy reflects loss of elastic fibres with fibrosis and increased collagen rather than simple thickening
It is a major posterior contributor to degenerative spinal canal stenosis, combining with disc bulging and facet hypertrophy to produce the trefoil-shaped canal of lumbar stenosis
The thickened ligament buckles and infolds into the canal during extension and axial loading, producing a dynamic component to stenosis that worsens on standing and walking and eases on flexion
This dynamic behaviour underlies neurogenic claudication, with the shopping-trolley sign and relief on sitting or leaning forward

It should be distinguished from ossification of the ligamentum flavum, a distinct entity that predominantly affects the thoracic spine and can cause myelopathy, particularly in East Asian populations and in association with diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis
MRI shows the thickened low-signal ligament indenting the dorsolateral thecal sac, and the degree of thickening correlates with the severity of canal narrowing
Definitive treatment of symptomatic stenosis is surgical decompression to remove the hypertrophied ligament, with conservative measures reserved for milder disease
reference.pathophysiology: Ligamentum flavum hypertrophy is a degenerative process in which chronic mechanical stress and low-grade inflammation drive fibrosis of the normally elastic ligament. Repetitive loading, disc-height loss and segmental instability increase strain on the ligament and stimulate fibroblasts through transforming growth factor beta and other profibrotic mediators, leading to loss of elastic fibres, disorganised collagen deposition, scarring and sometimes calcification or ossification. Reduced disc height also allows the ligament to buckle and infold into the canal rather than stretch. The combined static bulk and dynamic buckling narrow the central canal and lateral recesses, compressing neural elements and, with axial loading and extension, producing intermittent ischaemia of the cauda equina or nerve roots that manifests as neurogenic claudication.
additionalDifferentials: Ossification of the ligamentum flavum, particularly in the thoracic spine
Ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament
Degenerative disc herniation or bulge causing anterior canal compromise
Facet joint hypertrophy or synovial cyst compressing the lateral recess
Vascular claudication as a cause of exertional leg symptoms
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the affected spinal region to measure ligamentum flavum thickness and grade canal and recess stenosis
CT to demonstrate any calcification or ossification and bony anatomy for surgical planning
Standing and flexion-extension radiographs to assess dynamic instability and spondylolisthesis
Upright or axially loaded MRI where dynamic stenosis is suspected but supine imaging is equivocal
Ankle-brachial pressure index or vascular studies to exclude peripheral arterial disease
Electrophysiological studies where a peripheral neuropathy or radiculopathy needs clarification
redFlags: Progressive myelopathy with hyperreflexia and gait disturbance, especially with thoracic ossification
Cauda equina syndrome with saddle anaesthesia and bladder or bowel dysfunction
Rapidly progressive or profound lower-limb weakness
New or nocturnal back pain with systemic features suggesting infection or malignancy rather than degenerative stenosis
reference.prognosis: Symptomatic degenerative stenosis due to ligamentum flavum hypertrophy tends to progress slowly, and surgical decompression reliably relieves neurogenic claudication in appropriately selected patients, although established myelopathy from thoracic ossification recovers less predictably.
pitfalls: Relying on supine MRI alone and underestimating dynamic stenosis that only manifests on standing or extension
Confusing neurogenic with vascular claudication and missing peripheral arterial disease
Overlooking thoracic ossification of the ligamentum flavum as a cause of myelopathy
Attributing all symptoms to ligamentum flavum thickening when a synovial cyst, disc herniation or instability is the dominant lesion
references: Apley and Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma
